opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it comes down to what you actually need the model to do when you're building an agent that has to achieve goals in the world. Generative approaches, whether that's pixel-level video generation or autoregressive token prediction, are trained to reconstruct every detail of the observation. That's a really powerful learning signal, and you get beautiful samples out of it, but a lot of the model's capacity ends up going toward things that are fundamentally unpredictable or just irrelevant to the task: the exact texture of leaves blowing in the background, the precise lighting flicker. If you're trying to plan a sequence of actions to pick up an object, none of that matters.

With latent prediction models, the joint-embedding predictive architectures like I-JEPA and V-JEPA that we've been working on, the idea is that you predict in a learned representation space rather than in the input space. The encoder is free to discard information that isn't predictable, and the predictor only has to model the dynamics of the stuff that matters at an abstract level. In our experience that gives you representations that are more semantic, more efficient to train, and much better suited to planning, because when you roll out a world model for model-predictive control, you're searching over actions and evaluating outcomes many, many times. Doing that in a compact latent space is dramatically cheaper than generating full frames.

That said, I don't think it's a strict either-or. Generative models are very good when the output itself is the product, when you need a human to look at the video or read the text. And there are real open challenges on the latent side: avoiding representation collapse, making long-horizon predictions that stay coherent, and specifying goals in a latent space in a way that's grounded and interpretable. But for the specific problem of an agent that needs to understand, predict, and act toward a goal, my view is that predicting in an abstract representation space is the more promising path. You want the model spending its effort on the consequences of actions, not on rendering pixels.

r001.rationale: The response says generative models reconstruct every observation detail and devote substantial capacity to unpredictable, irrelevant details, while latent prediction can discard information that is not predictable.

r002.rationale: It says latent representations are more efficient to train and that planning in compact latent space is dramatically cheaper than generating full frames.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, the core distinction is really about what you're asking the model to spend its capacity on. A generative approach, whether it's pixel reconstruction or autoregressive prediction, is asking the model to predict every detail of the future: every leaf blowing in the wind, every texture, every bit of sensor noise. And the problem is that most of that detail is fundamentally unpredictable and, more importantly, irrelevant to the goal the agent is trying to achieve.

So when you train a world model generatively, a lot of the representational capacity and a lot of the loss signal end up devoted to things that don't matter for planning. You're modeling the chaos instead of modeling the structure. And for a goal-driven agent, what you really care about is the structure: how does the state of the world change as a consequence of my actions, at the level of abstraction that's relevant for deciding what to do next?

That's where latent prediction comes in. With something like JEPA, the joint embedding predictive architecture, you're predicting in representation space rather than in input space. The model learns an encoder that can discard the unpredictable or irrelevant information, and then a predictor that captures the dynamics at that abstract level. So you get to choose, in a sense, what to be uncertain about and what to ignore entirely. That's a much more natural fit for planning, because you can do model predictive control in that latent space, roll out candidate action sequences, and compare predicted outcomes against a goal embedding without ever having to render pixels.

Now, I don't want to be dismissive of generative models. They've been incredibly successful, and there are settings where you genuinely want the full distribution, for simulation, for content creation, for cases where the details are the point. And there are real challenges on the latent side, particularly around collapse, where the easy solution is for the encoder to map everything to a constant. A lot of the engineering effort in this line of work goes into preventing that in a principled way.

But if the question is specifically about building agents that reason toward goals in the physical world, I'd argue latent prediction is the more scalable path. It aligns the learning objective with what the agent actually needs, which is an abstract, actionable model of consequences, rather than a photorealistic one. And empirically, what we've seen is that models trained this way learn representations that are more useful for downstream planning and control with far less compute than their generative counterparts, precisely because they're not wasting effort on the parts of the world that don't carry signal.

r001.rationale: The response says generative models predict every detail, including fundamentally unpredictable ones, while latent prediction can discard irrelevant information.

r002.rationale: It calls latent prediction the more scalable path and says these models support planning and control with far less compute than generative counterparts.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is, what does an agent need to predict in order to act? A generative model tries to predict observations themselves—for example, what the next video frame will look like. That’s a powerful capability, but it also means modeling a lot of details that may not matter for the goal: textures, lighting, or exactly how a background moves.

With latent prediction, the idea is to predict in a representation space where you can retain the information that matters for making decisions without reconstructing every pixel. If you can predict how that representation changes as a function of your actions, then you potentially have a world model you can use for planning: consider different actions and ask which ones bring you closer to a goal.

The challenge is learning the right representation. You can’t just throw away detail indiscriminately, because something that’s irrelevant for one task might be essential for another. So latent prediction isn’t automatically a solution to building a goal-driven agent. You still need representations that capture the relevant dynamics, action-conditioned predictions, and a way to evaluate progress toward the goal.

I see these approaches as potentially complementary. Generative models are useful when you need to produce detailed outputs. But for the internal predictions an agent makes while planning, I think there’s a strong argument for operating in an abstract representation space.

r001.rationale: The response says generative models must model details that may not matter to the goal, but it does not state that this means substantially more uncertainty than with latent prediction models.

r002.rationale: The response argues that abstract representations may be useful for planning, but does not predict that latent prediction models will be substantially more efficient for learning goal-driven agents.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: what does an agent actually need to predict in order to act? A generative model tries to predict observations in a lot of detail. If you’re predicting video, that can mean accounting for textures, lighting, and other things that may have very little to do with whether an action gets you closer to your goal. And a lot of those details are inherently unpredictable.

With latent prediction, the idea is to predict in a representation space where you can retain the information that matters without having to reconstruct every pixel. If you can learn a representation that captures the state of the world and how it changes with your actions, you could use that to evaluate possible actions and plan toward a goal.

But the important caveat is that learning a good predictive representation doesn’t automatically give you a goal-driven agent. You still need to demonstrate that it preserves the information needed for control, that you can predict the consequences of actions, and that planning with those predictions actually works. So I see latent prediction as a promising foundation, with a lot still to establish between learning representations and building agents that reliably achieve goals.

r001.rationale: The response says generative models must predict detailed observations, including irrelevant details that are inherently unpredictable, while latent prediction can avoid reconstructing every pixel. This communicates the greater uncertainty burden of generative modeling.

r002.rationale: The response calls latent prediction a promising foundation but does not predict that it will make learning goal-driven agents substantially more efficient.
